questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The objection to one currency across many budgets
questions.learningObjective: Identify why one currency struggles across divergent national budgets
questions.stem: Ticket 01 asks why one currency struggles across many budgets; pick the core flaw in the team's reasoning.

options.text: Fiscal shocks hit regions without offsetting transfers
Exchange rates can still adjust after monetary union
options.misconception: assumes rates can still adjust after union

options.text: Inflation always rises under a single currency
options.misconception: confuses price level with inflation variance

options.text: Trade balances automatically equalise across members

questions.explanation: A single currency removes exchange-rate adjustment, so asymmetric fiscal shocks persist without transfers. Trade does not auto-equalise.
questions.hint: Think about shock absorption without devaluation.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Moving the rates inside the band in 1992
questions.learningObjective: Explain why widening the band in 1992 relieved currency pressure
questions.stem: Ticket 02 notes a 1992 band widening; what immediate effect did it have on speculative attacks?

options.text: It increased the cost of defending the peg
options.misconception: confuses band width with intervention cost

options.text: It gave central banks room to cut rates
It forced instant devaluation of all currencies
It ended the exchange rate mechanism entirely

questions.explanation: A wider band let rates move further, reducing the need for punitive rate hikes to defend parities. It did not abolish the mechanism.
questions.hint: Wider bands mean less defence pressure.

questions.learningObjective: List convergence criteria a state must meet before adopting the currency
questions.stem: Ticket 03 shows a candidate state's inflation at 4.2% and debt at 70% of GDP; which criterion is failed?
questions.explanation: Inflation must be within 1.5 points of the best three; 4.2% likely exceeds it. Debt at 70% can be acceptable if declining. Only inflation clearly fails.
questions.hint: Check the inflation reference value first.

questions.stem: Ticket 04 asks for the legal text that fixes the bank's price-stability mandate; give the exemplar answer.

answer.exemplar: The statute names price stability as the primary objective and grants operational independence, so the bank sets rates without political instruction.

questions.explanation: The bank's statute makes price stability the primary objective and protects operational independence from political instruction. Rate setting follows from that mandate.
questions.hint: Name the statute and its primary objective.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Decisions taken where no voters elect anyone
questions.learningObjective: Identify the democratic deficit in unelected decision making

stimulus.body: The council meets behind closed doors and appoints commissioners who answer to no electorate. Parliament votes but cannot initiate legislation. Citizens have no direct say in rate setting.

questions.stem: Ticket 05 quotes an excerpt on unelected bodies; what democratic deficit does it highlight?

options.text: Parliament has too much legislative power
Central bank rates are set by elected officials
options.misconception: confuses appointed with elected rate setters

options.text: Voters cannot remove the commission directly

questions.explanation: Unelected commissioners and a parliament that cannot initiate laws create a democratic deficit. Closed meetings do not improve accountability.
questions.hint: Focus on who voters can remove.

questions.learningObjective: Apply subsidiarity to decide the right level of action
questions.stem: Ticket 10 asks for the rule that action belongs as close to the citizen as possible; state it.

answer.exemplar: Subsidiarity means decisions are taken at the lowest competent level, with higher levels acting only when objectives cannot be met locally.

questions.explanation: Subsidiarity places action at the lowest competent level and reserves higher-level action for objectives local levels cannot achieve. It is not centralisation.

questions.topic: The objection to one currency across many budgets
questions.learningObjective: Identify a policy response to asymmetric shocks under one currency

stimulus.body: The union has no large budget to transfer funds between regions. Labour moves slowly across borders. Wages rarely fall in depressed areas. These gaps make a single currency painful.

options.misconception: jumps to an extreme not implied

questions.explanation: The excerpt highlights missing transfers, slow labour mobility, and rigid wages, implying fiscal transfers are needed. Rate hikes would worsen depressions.
questions.hint: The gaps point to missing transfers.

questions.topic: A bank's losses become the currency's problem
questions.learningObjective: Synthesise a bank-sovereign doom loop

stimulus.body: Banks hold large amounts of their own government's debt. When that debt falls in value, bank capital erodes. Weaker banks then need state support, which worsens the debt. The cycle feeds on itself.

questions.stem: Ticket 29 quotes an excerpt on a doom loop; what cycle does it describe?

options.text: Debt always rises because of banks alone
Bank and sovereign weaken each other
The loop is broken by printing money

questions.explanation: The loop runs both ways: falling sovereign debt erodes bank capital, and bank rescues worsen sovereign debt. It is a feedback cycle.

stimulus.body: A candidate must keep its currency within the normal fluctuation margins for two years without severe tensions. Stability is tested in practice, not on paper. Devaluations during the period disqualify.

stimulus.body: When banks fail, governments rescue them. The rescue raises public debt. Higher debt lowers bond prices, hurting banks that hold those bonds. Each round deepens the other's trouble.
